neurological_exam.additional: Patient presented with 1-week fever, confusion, and inability to walk. Initial diagnosis: pneumonia + possible bacterial meningitis. Treated empirically with ceftriaxone, vancomycin, ampicillin, and acyclovir (broad encephalitis coverage). Chest X-ray and CT: patchy left base infiltrate — pneumonia. Facial droop with arm weakness triggered 'stroke notification' — head CT unremarkable twice. Rapid deterioration required MICU intubation.

patient.chief_complaint: One-week fever with confusion, inability to walk, and ascending paralysis — initially presenting as meningoencephalitis, with progressive neurological deterioration requiring intubation.
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. G. is a 67-year-old woman presenting with a 1-week history of intermittent fever. Three days before this admission, she was seen in the emergency department for presumed community-acquired pneumonia and treated with levofloxacin. She returned 3 days later with worsening fever (101°F), generalized weakness, inability to walk, confusion, and difficulty expressing herself. She denied sick contacts, new travel, or animal exposures. On exam: crackles in right middle and lower lung fields. Chest X-ray showed patchy left lower lobe density. She was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for suspected community-acquired pneumonia. Neurological assessment on admission showed mild confusion oriented to person, time, and place, with weakness but still able to move extremities — she could not lift her arms more than 10 inches. A head CT was unremarkable. The following day she was oriented only to person, had rigid neck, incomprehensible speech but followed simple commands, and showed asymmetric left facial droop with greater left arm weakness. A second head CT was unremarkable. Later that day she became unresponsive, required emergency intubation, and was transferred to the MICU. This dramatic deterioration — progressing from walking difficulty to near-coma requiring intubation within 48 hours — was initially evaluated as complicated meningoencephalitis. Multiple antibiotics including vancomycin, ampicillin, and acyclovir were added empirically. Neurology was consulted after LP revealed elevated protein with normal WBC — the pattern pointing away from bacterial meningitis and toward GBS.

critical_actions: LP is the pivotal diagnostic test — albumino-cytologic dissociation distinguishes GBS from meningitis and is the finding that redirects therapy from empiric antibiotics to IVIG
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a recognized GBS trigger — the pneumonia and GBS share the same trigger; treat both
Macrolide antibiotics (azithromycin, clarithromycin) are contraindicated with QTc >460 ms in GBS autonomic context — switch to doxycycline for Mycoplasma
Levofloxacin (used initially for pneumonia) is also QT-prolonging — also contraindicated; use beta-lactam + doxycycline
GBS with meningoencephalitis presentation: the confusion in GBS is from SIADH, fever from concurrent pneumonia, and encephalopathy — the LP result is the discriminating test
key_reasoning_points: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the third most common GBS trigger (after Campylobacter and EBV) — Mycoplasma atypical pneumonia + GBS can present concurrently
CSF albumino-cytologic dissociation is the key finding that shifts the diagnosis from meningoencephalitis to GBS — normal WBC with elevated protein is NOT meningitis
SIADH in GBS (hyponatremia sodium 132) can cause confusion that mimics encephalitis — the meningoencephalitis presentation of GBS is a recognized clinical trap
Macrolide antibiotics are contraindicated in GBS with QTc prolongation — Mycoplasma treatment should use doxycycline or tetracycline
The 'stroke notification' for unilateral facial droop + arm weakness was appropriate — two negative CT heads correctly excluded stroke before LP was prioritized
